content: Magnesium hydroxide, when administered orally, can interact with various drugs and substances, leading to altered absorption, bioavailability, or pharmacodynamic effects. Below are the detailed interactions: 1. Magnesium hydroxide and baloxavir marboxil: Magnesium hydroxide reduces the absorption of baloxavir marboxil in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract due to cation binding. This interaction decreases plasma levels of baloxavir marboxil. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 2. Magnesium hydroxide and demeclocycline: Magnesium hydroxide inhibits the GI absorption of demeclocycline, leading to reduced plasma levels. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Avoid co-administration or consider alternative therapy. 3. Magnesium hydroxide and doxycycline: Magnesium hydroxide decreases the absorption of doxycycline in the GI tract, reducing its effectiveness. This interaction applies only to oral forms. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 4. Magnesium hydroxide and eltrombopag: Magnesium hydroxide inhibits the GI absorption of eltrombopag, significantly reducing its plasma levels. This interaction is contraindicated. Separate administration by at least 4 hours. 5. Magnesium hydroxide and infigratinib: Magnesium hydroxide reduces the absorption of infigratinib in the GI tract. If co-administration with an acid-reducing agent cannot be avoided, administer infigratinib 2 hours before and after the antacid. 6. Magnesium hydroxide and minocycline: Magnesium hydroxide inhibits the GI absorption of minocycline, reducing its plasma levels. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 7. Magnesium hydroxide and oxytetracycline: Magnesium hydroxide decreases the absorption of oxytetracycline in the GI tract. Avoid co-administration or consider alternative therapy. 8. Magnesium hydroxide and pazopanib: Magnesium hydroxide increases gastric pH, reducing the solubility and bioavailability of pazopanib. Avoid co-administration with drugs that raise gastric pH. Short-acting antacids may be used, but separate dosing by several hours. 9. Magnesium hydroxide and ponatinib: Magnesium hydroxide increases gastric pH, reducing the bioavailability of ponatinib. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 10. Magnesium hydroxide and potassium phosphates (IV): Magnesium hydroxide binds dietary phosphate, reducing serum phosphate concentrations. Use alternatives if available. 11. Magnesium hydroxide and raltegravir: Magnesium-containing antacids reduce raltegravir plasma levels when taken within 6 hours of raltegravir. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 12. Magnesium hydroxide and sotorasib: Magnesium hydroxide inhibits the GI absorption of sotorasib. If co-administration with an acid-reducing agent cannot be avoided, administer sotorasib 4 hours before or 10 hours after the antacid. 13. Magnesium hydroxide and tetracycline: Magnesium hydroxide reduces the absorption of tetracycline in the GI tract. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 14. Magnesium hydroxide and pancrelipase: Antacids like magnesium hydroxide may negate the beneficial effects of pancrelipase enzymes. Use caution and monitor therapy. 15. Magnesium hydroxide and penicillamine: Magnesium hydroxide inhibits the GI absorption of penicillamine. Separate administration by at least 2 hours. 16. Magnesium hydroxide and pexidartinib: Magnesium hydroxide reduces the absorption of pexidartinib. Separate administration by 2 hours before or after the antacid. 17. Magnesium hydroxide and riociguat: Magnesium hydroxide inhibits the GI absorption of riociguat. Separate administration by at least 1 hour. 18. Magnesium hydroxide and sarecycline: Magnesium hydroxide reduces the absorption of sarecycline. Separate dosing of tetracyclines from magnesium-containing products. 19. Magnesium hydroxide and sodium phosphates (IV): Magnesium hydroxide binds dietary phosphate, reducing serum phosphate concentrations. Use alternatives if available. 20. Magnesium hydroxide and vismodegib: Drugs that increase gastric pH, such as magnesium hydroxide, alter vismodegib solubility and reduce its bioavailability. Use caution and monitor therapy. 21. Mineral oil and beta-carotene: Mineral oil binds beta-carotene in the GI tract, reducing its absorption. Use caution and monitor therapy. 22. Mineral oil and vitamin D: Mineral oil reduces the absorption of vitamin D. Avoid concomitant use to prevent decreased vitamin D absorption. 23. Vitamin D and magnesium hydroxide: Vitamin D increases serum magnesium concentrations, particularly in patients with renal impairment. Avoid combined use in patients with chronic renal failure. 24. Amikacin and magnesium hydroxide: Amikacin increases renal clearance of magnesium hydroxide, reducing its levels. The clinical significance is unknown. 25. Amiloride and magnesium hydroxide: Amiloride decreases renal clearance of magnesium hydroxide, increasing its levels. The clinical significance is unknown. 26. Amphotericin B deoxycholate and magnesium hydroxide: Amphotericin B increases renal clearance of magnesium hydroxide, reducing its levels. The clinical significance is unknown. 27. Mineral oil and digoxin: Mineral oil inhibits the GI absorption of digoxin. Use caution and monitor therapy. 28. Mineral oil and anticoagulants (e.g., heparin, enoxaparin, fondaparinux): Mineral oil reduces the absorption of these agents in the GI tract. The clinical significance is unknown. 29. Mineral oil and oral contraceptives (e.g., ethinyl estradiol, levonorgestrel): Mineral oil reduces the absorption of these agents. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 30.
